When Joel Paxton posted a video of a set of gates on social media, he attracted hundreds of comments from people who disliked them. But among the almost one million people who watched the clip was a set designer, working on HBO's new Harry Potter series. Soon afterwards, Paxton was contacted about the gates and found himself getting a behind-the-scenes glimpse of one of television's most anticipated productions. "We had an interesting set of gates that came through the door, and I'd say they're quite a unique piece," said Paxton, who runs Rustique Living in Sandon, Staffordshire. "We did a little video on that, and it just blew up for some reason." Among the online comments were reactions ranging from "yuck" to "disgusting", with some social media users questioning why anyone would want to buy the gates. OpenSynth is an open source community hosted by LF Energy that is democratising access to synthetic energy demand data. Access to smart meter data is essential to rapid and successful energy transitions. Researchers, modelers and policymakers need to understand how energy demand profiles are changing, in a system that requires greater real time optimization of demand and supply on the grid. Yet current global energy modeling and policymaking is still largely based on static and highly aggregated data from the past – when energy flowed in one direction, consumer profiles were relatively predictable, and power generation was highly controllable. The major challenge is that access to demand data is highly restrictive, as a result of privacy protections. Rather than joining industry calls to unlock raw smart meter data through existing mechanisms, by tackling current data regulations and smart meter legislation, OpenSynth believes generating synthetic data is the fastest way to achieve widespread, global access to smart meter datasets. How People with Type 2 Diabetes Can Live Longer For Everyone Nov. 16, 2026 Key points Life expectancy is known as the number of years a person is expected to live. At age 50, life expectancy is 6 years shorter for people with type 2 diabetes than for people without diabetes. By meeting type 2 diabetes treatment goals, life expectancy can increase by 3 years, or for some, as much as 10 years. What did this study examine? This study measured average increases in life expectancy years for people with type 2 diabetes who met four different treatment goals. Well before dawn Peter Raven walks out the back door of his house in St. Louis and up a path to a low, modern building faced in glass that in daylight reflects the surrounding grounds of the oldest institution of its kind in the United States. For the past 19 years Raven has been director of the Missouri Botanical Garden , which he has transformed into a landscape of exceptional beauty. His alarm at what is happening to tropical rain forests, however, has caused the garden to transcend aesthetics and become one of the world's leading centers for tropical botanical research. pages.text: How Premier League's big six keep getting richer and richer - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images By Dale Johnson Football issues correspondent Published 3 hours ago Ten games into the Premier League season, four of the top six spots are occupied by 'big six' clubs. In pure financial terms, it should come as no surprise. The six biggest clubs - Manchester United , Liverpool , Manchester City , Arsenal , Tottenham and Chelsea - now generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the division's other teams. And the gap is growing. Every season. BBC Sport breaks down how the finances of the big six have exploded, examines new trends and the impact on the transfer market, and asks how much it really matters. Big six get richer and the gap grows Companies put their money where supporters are prepared to spend it. It is a simple fact of business in every country, a reality of football's food chain. In England, Liverpool , Arsenal and Manchester United traditionally dominated viewing figures, column inches, shirt sales and sponsorship. Over the past 20 years they have been joined by Chelsea , Manchester City and Tottenham . This group of clubs now generate so much money it is hard to imagine how they can fail in the long term - even factoring in short-term performance issues. Let's look at how the gap has grown. How RSV Spreads Feb. 20, 2026 Español What to know Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) can spread when an infected person coughs or sneezes, by direct contact with someone who has RSV, or by touching a contaminated surface. In most regions of the United States, RSV season generally starts during the fall and peaks in the winter. Everyone can take action to help prevent the spread of RSV. RSV transmission RSV can spread when: A person who has RSV coughs or sneezes near you. Droplets from a cough or sneeze that contain the virus get in your eyes, nose, or mouth. You have direct contact with someone with RSV, like kissing the face of a child with RSV. You touch a surface that has the virus on it, like a doorknob, and then touch your face before washing your hands. People of any age can get RSV, but typically most people get RSV for the first time as an infant or toddler. Nearly all children will get RSV before their second birthday. However, repeat infections may occur throughout life. Who is at risk? Infants, some young children , and adults who are older or have certain risk factors are at increased risk of severe RSV illness. October 4, 2024 How Salmonella Infections Happen Key points Salmonella can spread to people in many ways. Most often, the bacteria spread through food. Salmonella also can spread through water, animals, people, and other ways. You can take steps to help prevent infection. Some common sources of infection Contaminated food Salmonella most often spread to people through contaminated food. CDC estimates that most Salmonella infections are linked to chicken, fruits, pork, seeded vegetables (such as tomatoes), other produce (such as nuts), beef, and turkey. But any food can become contaminated, even processed foods (such as flour). Keep Reading: How Food Gets Contaminated: The Food Production Chain Cross-contamination Foods that are contaminated with Salmonella can spread germs to other foods if they are not kept separated. Unwashed hands, chopping boards, and knives can also spread germs from these foods to other foods. By Erin Blakemore Published October 23, 2023 • 7 min read It’s a moment that never fails to stop Oscar Nilsson in his tracks—an instant in which archaeology and art collide. After many months spent reconstructing the facial structure of a long-dead human in his Stockholm studio, Nilsson begins to apply a layer of “skin” to his latest silicone bust. He uses ever-tinier needles to create wrinkles and pores, applies paints that capture the essence of a human epidermis, and pokes infinitesimal hairs onto his creation. Then he opens its eyelids. “It immediately becomes a face,” says Nilsson, a trained archaeologist and sculptor who specializes in 3D facial reconstructions of ancient humans. “After more than 20 years, it’s still a great day in the studio.” ( Archaeologists give him skulls—Oscar Nilsson brings them to life .) Background SQLite is a software library that translates high-level disk I/O requests generated by an application into low-level I/O operations that can be carried out by the operating system. The application constructs high-level I/O requests using the SQL language . SQLite translates each high-level SQL statement into a sequence of many low-level I/O requests (open a file, read a few bytes from a file, write a few bytes into a file, etc.) that do the work requested by the SQL. An application program could do all its disk I/O by direct calls to operating system I/O routines or by using a key/value storage engine like Berkeley DB or RocksDB (to name but two). But there are advantages to using a higher-level interface based on the SQL language. SQL is a very high-level language. A few lines of SQL can replace hundreds or thousands of lines of procedural code. SQL thus reduces the amount of work needed to develop and maintain the application, and thereby helps to reduce the number of bugs in the application. SQL and SQLite are transactional . ALBUM By Editors of National Geographic Published September 21, 2026 In 1842 the Treaty of Nanjing put an end to the First Opium War but forced China to open several “treaty ports,” which allowed European merchants to settle in Shanghai , then a fishing village not far from the mouth of the Yangtze River. British, French, American, and later Japanese settlers established themselves in enclaves known as concessions that were completely autonomous territories within the city. Their arrival, along with refugees of the Taiping Rebellion and later Jewish refugees of World War II, marked the beginning of Shanghai’s transformation into a strategic commercial, financial, and industrial hub. Westerners remained a minority (150,000 in the early 1940s), but they left a deep mark on the city, especially in the Bund, its historic district located on the waterfront of the Huangpu River (pictured above). The inventor of this style of sun compass, Albert H. Bumstead, was a renowned tinkerer and the National Geographic Society's first chief cartographer. Mark Thiessen, NGM staff By Brian Kevin Published December 30, 2025 The magnetized needle of a conventional compass wants to align with Earth’s magnetic field—helpful, unless you’re near the poles, where the field tugs straight downward, rendering magnetic compasses useless. Pilot and National Geographic Explorer Richard E. Byrd, who hoped to fly over the North Pole in the summer of 1925, lamented this during a pre-trip address to the National Geographic Society, and his gripe sent chief cartographer Albert H. Bumstead tinkering. Bumstead developed a novel piece of hardware, a bit like a swiveling watch. Incline it to match one’s latitude and the single, 24-hour hand tracks the sun across the sky. Since the sun at northern latitudes sits due south at noon, an Arctic aviator can align the hand with the sun and set a compass dial by the timepiece. Simple. Elegant. Byrd took one to the Arctic in 1925 and again in ’26. He returned it to the cartographer engraved: “To Albert H. Bumstead. How This Self-Taught Web Developer Went Straight to a Master's Degree Written by Amanda Wicks • Updated on Feb 26, 2026 Kaushik Muthyalu began learning about computers at age 10, which enabled him to take advantage of CU Boulder's performance-based admission. Some students begin learning a subject at such a young age that more traditional kinds of higher education, like a bachelor’s degree , can’t always meet their needs. They end up spending four or five years reinforcing what they already know. That was the case with Kaushik Muthyalu, a web developer in India. He began learning how to code at age 10 and two years later moved on to web development. As the prospect of university loomed, Muthyalu had a strong foundation in computer science, but higher education didn’t meet him where he was. “I studied game development in college for one year before dropping out because I didn’t find it as interesting as I thought it would be,” he explained. “I felt that I wasn’t learning anything useful that I couldn’t learn by myself.” After leaving his bachelor’s program, Muthyalu wasn’t sure what to do. His dad approached him with an opportunity to work as a web developer on a new financial app he wanted to launch. Muthyalu spent the next five years working for his father, but when it came time to explore other opportunities, he found that his lack of degree hurt his prospects. “That’s when I decided to go back to school,” he said.

If you have something sensitive to share with us, here’s how to get in touch. Confidential tips Journalists work closely with readers like you to investigate stories in the public interest. While no communication system is foolproof we go to great lengths to protect your identity. If you’re ready to share information with a journalist, you’re in the right place, and we will treat you as a confidential journalistic source. We rely on people sharing tips in the public interest – and we’re grateful that you’re thinking about getting in touch. Composing your message We’re unlikely to pursue a lead unless we think it may lead to a news story, and we can't act on information that is vague or speculative. Our job is to hold power to account, to reveal institutional or systemic failings and to report on topics that are genuinely newsworthy. Please be clear, detailed and specific about your tip, why you think it matters, and what evidence you have. Facts: Specifics are critical, such as names, locations and dates. Chris Schalkx, Kintzing By Kristin Braswell Published October 20, 2026 Separated by a narrow strip of sea, the Malaysian state of Penang has dual personalities: On Penang Island, travelers can explore the historic streets of George Town, the capital city, before heading to rainforest-fringed beaches. On the mainland Seberang Perai, across the Penang Strait, traditional villages and winding mangrove rivers sit alongside industrial hubs. Chinese, Indian, Burmese, Arab, and European immigrants have shaped the cuisine, architecture, and religious identity of Penang, which was once a key trading post linking the Pacific and Indian Oceans. In George Town today, luxury hotels are housed in former Chinese merchant family estates, well-preserved colonial buildings, and narrow alleyways lined with murals and street food hawkers, giving the city a metropolitan pulse. pages.text: How to Experience Iceland's Fire and Ice in Reykjavík | National Geographic TRAVEL How to Experience Iceland's Fire and Ice in Reykjavík Iceland’s capital lives up to the country’s nickname — the Land of Fire and Ice — with geologically rooted cultural curiosities, bathing pools, bars and restaurants The design of Hallgrímskirkja, Reykjavík’s main church, is said to have been inspired by the country’s mountains. Getty By Daniel Stables Published October 22, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). The world’s northernmost capital, Reykjavík is a culturally vibrant city, home to around one third of Iceland’s population. Yet, it still feels close to the duelling forces of nature that define the country’s life and landscape: glaciers and snow-capped mountains above ground; and an infernal volcanism seething below the surface, heating geothermal pools and hot springs. Clues to this unique dynamic are everywhere in Reykjavík. It runs almost exclusively on geothermal power — the only capital city in the world to do so. The tap water, naturally filtered through mazes of volcanic rock, is preternaturally pure and good for the skin (you’ll soon get used to the slightly eggy, sulphurous smell). Galleries host displays of artwork hewn from glacier ice, while immersive exhibits take you deep into the belly of the Earth. Some of the country’s most spectacular bathing pools are found right here, too, ensuring your time in Reykjavík will be, quite literally, immersive. pages.text: How to Experience St Moritz’s Snow Polo World Cup Weekend | National Geographic By Emma Al-Mousawi Published November 14, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). For one weekend in late January, frozen Lake St Moritz, encircled by Switzerland’s snow-heaped Engadin Alps, becomes the glittering stage for one of polo’s most prestigious events: the Snow Polo World Cup St Moritz. Sunglass-clad spectators in cashmere, elegant coats and designer puffer jackets gather as champagne flutes clink and oysters are shucked. On the ice, six teams of white-slacked players thunder across the 200-metre pitch, competing for the coveted trophy against the dazzling backdrop of one of Europe’s oldest and most exclusive ski resorts. Polo traces its origins back more than two millennia to the grasslands of Persia, but its snowy incarnation is decidedly younger. It was conceived here just over 40 years ago by Reto Gaudenzi, a local player and founder of Switzerland’s first polo team. Undeterred by the fact that polo had never been played on snow, he experimented with hoof grips and a larger, slower orange ball. A successful trial followed in 1984; a year later, the world’s first snow polo tournament was staged on the lake before more than 1,000 spectators. Today, the three-day event draws crowds of 26,000 — and dozens of private jets. Forty grooms tend 120 ponies in heated stables, while three daily matches unfold on snow-covered ice at least 50cm thick. pages.description: Passengers aboard the Ultramarine can feel the Arctic wind on their faces as they get up close with Greenland’s biggest glaciers — and even take a plunge into the Atlantic’s icy waters.
pages.text: How to Explore Greenland by Luxury Expedition Ship | National Geographic TRAVEL How to Explore Greenland by Luxury Expedition Ship Passengers aboard the Ultramarine can feel the Arctic wind on their faces as they get up close with Greenland’s biggest glaciers — and even take a plunge into the Atlantic’s icy waters. Quark Expeditions’ heli-hiking trips use helicopters to reach remote hiking routes in southern Greenland. Michelle Sole, Quark Expeditions By Adrian Phillips Published November 6, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). “If you fall in, you’ll be there for thousands of years,” says a watchful guide as I crawl to the edge and stare into oblivion. The hole, drilled through the glacier by its own meltwater, is hundreds of metres deep. It’s part of an ice sheet two miles thick that covers 700,000sq miles of Greenland. Few come to this wilderness of sudden storms and treacherous crevasses. It’s mainly tough-skinned adventurers, seasoned Inuit hunters — plus a handful of tourists like me. Such an otherworldly spot is, for the first time, within reach of tough-skinned and soft-skinned alike. Our ship — the Ultramarine — has a pair of twin-engined helicopters that extend its reach far beyond the fjords of southern Greenland. “I like to pretend you’re holding gin and tonics,” says our smooth-talking helicopter pilot, after flying seven miles north from the ship and landing on the glacier with the gentlest of thuds. “There now. pages.title: How to Explore the Indian Ocean Through Its Spices | National Geographic
pages.description: Once among the world’s most valuable commodities, spices transformed the Indian Ocean, enriching empires while weaving together the cultures, cuisines and communities of distant shores. Today, travellers can still follow those ancient routes through fragrant plantation visits, cooking classes and market tours.
pages.text: How to Explore the Indian Ocean Through Its Spices | National Geographic By Daniel Stables Published September 19, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Nowadays, most of us take spices for granted — a pinch of cinnamon in porridge, black pepper over pasta or cumin stirred into a curry. Yet for centuries these everyday ingredients shaped the course of history. The trade in black pepper facilitated cultural and economic intermixing between ancient Rome and India, while camels pulled frankincense caravans across the deserts that separated Africa and Asia, taking with them ideas, recipes, music and language. Today, these influences can still be felt in many countries, offering a fascinating, and often delicious, theme through which to explore a place. Browse the Spice Souks of Muscat, Oman Located on the Arabian Sea between Saudi Arabia, Yemen and the UAE, the seafaring nation of Oman has long been a link between East Africa, India and Southeast Asia. That story is told in the spice section of Muttrah Souk, the Omani capital’s historic covered market, where technicolour cones of powdered ginger, turmeric and cumin sit alongside piles of frankincense rocks, bundled strands of saffron, and less familiar items like loomi — black, sun-dried limes. The air hangs particularly heavy with the scent of frankincense, which Omanis use to perfume their homes, cars and traditional robes. pages.text: How to Explore the Pantanal | National Geographic A school of fish and a hungry caiman in the waters of the Pantanal region Photograph by Luciano Candisani, National Geographic TRAVEL How to Explore the Pantanal Explore the Pantanal from all corners with this guide to the beauty of this national park and UNESCO World Heritage site. By Avery Stonich Published August 4, 2016 • 4 min read The Pantanal is the world’s largest wetland , pooling over 81,000 square miles (210,000 square kilometers)—an area nearly the size of Kansas—in the center of South America, mostly in central-western Brazil and straddling the borders of Paraguay and Bolivia. Often overshadowed by the Amazon to the north, the Pantanal quietly harbors the highest concentration of wildlife in South America . It’s part national park and part UNESCO World Heritage site , and it’s considered a critical region of the world by the World Wildlife Fund, which estimates that 325 species of fish, 159 species of mammals, 656 species of birds, 53 species of amphibians, and 98 species of reptiles live in this hotbed of biodiversity. pages.text: How to explore the tropical side of Japan in Okinawa | National Geographic TRAVEL How to explore the tropical side of Japan in Okinawa With its laid-back seafaring culture and unique wildlife, the Yaeyama archipelago in Japan’s far southern Okinawa prefecture reveals a different side to Japan. The traditional Okinawan sabani boats were historically used for fishing and travelling between islands. Photograph by James Whitlow Delano By Georgia Stephens Published January 7, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). It’s show time. Up heaves the sail, a concertina of heavy canvas pulled taut against the creaking wooden mast. It gulps the breeze that’s whisking cotton puffs of cloud out to sea. Black butterflies, big as sparrows, rise from the steep jungle at our backs as the droning of cicadas meets the surf raking the beach. The air is flower-scented, hot and heavy as water. Up comes the anchor, out come the paddles; the nose of the traditional sabani boat plunges into the waves. Any sailor leaving Ishigaki island needs to be absolutely certain of their course. Head north west, and the next landfall lies hundreds of miles away in China; east, and it’ll be the considerably farther-flung shores of Mexico. Here, in southern Okinawa Prefecture, Japan fizzles out in a spray of its remotest isles. Closer to Taiwan and the Philippines than the mainland and fed by warmer currents, the subtropical Yaeyama Islands, of which Ishigaki is a part, are unique within Japan.
